Dermatology · published research

Skin damage by infrared radiation

Experimental infrared exposure can increase erythema or selected oxidative and matrix markers under some conditions, while filtered or temperature-controlled studies report neutral findings. These studies do not show that nonthermal PBM causes chronic skin damage.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Experimental infrared exposure can increase erythema or selected oxidative and matrix markers under some conditions, while filtered or temperature-controlled studies report neutral findings. These studies do not show that nonthermal PBM causes chronic skin damage.

Summary of the Evidence

Sixteen publications address potential skin responses to infrared radiation: six reviews, one letter, and nine primary reports. The primary set includes four small human or mixed human-laboratory studies and five in-vitro fibroblast studies. No trial evaluates long-term clinical skin damage from therapeutic PBM. These records study possible effects of infrared exposure and should not be read as trials of PBM efficacy or proof that low-intensity treatment damages skin.

Human and clinical evidence

Phototesting in four people with solar urticaria found that infrared contributed to lesions induced by combined UVA and visible-light exposure. When infrared B was filtered from the source, three participants developed no lesion and one developed only a small wheal (de Gálvez et al. 2016). Other small acute exposure experiments reported increases in free-radical signals or ferritin after infrared-A exposure. In the small biopsy study, ferritin increased but frank DNA or extracellular-matrix damage was not observed. These short-term biomarkers do not establish chronic photoaging.

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified in this category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Some fibroblast studies report increased reactive oxygen species, matrix metalloproteinase-1, or extracellular-matrix disruption after infrared-A exposure. Other work using water-filtered or temperature-controlled infrared found little evidence of cytotoxicity or matrix damage. Differences in wavelength spectrum, irradiance, cumulative exposure, and heating help explain why the results do not all point in one direction.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The records concern infrared-A and infrared-B bands within the broader solar spectrum, with exposure conditions ranging from filtered phototesting to laboratory irradiation. Some experiments use much higher cumulative exposure or allow tissue heating; others control temperature. The category does not define a single therapeutic wavelength, dose, or schedule, and these exposures are not equivalent to a specified nonthermal PBM protocol.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a limited conclusion: sufficiently intense or heat-producing infrared exposure can alter acute skin responses and selected laboratory markers, but neutral findings also occur when spectrum and temperature differ. The studies do not show that appropriately dosed nonthermal red or near-infrared PBM causes chronic skin injury.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for acute skin responses to experimental infrared exposure No direct evidence that nonthermal PBM causes chronic skin damage
Publications and records16 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small acute human tests and laboratory studies report both increases in oxidative or matrix markers and neutral findings under filtered or temperature-controlled conditions. These experiments examine infrared exposure, often at solar or high-dose settings, rather than therapeutic PBM. Replicated human follow-up with quantified spectrum, dose, skin temperature, and clinical outcomes is needed to assess chronic risk.
